newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian 96/97 budget to disappoint - Access.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian 96/97 budget to disappoint - Access.

text.p: Leading Australian fiscal forecasters Access Economics said this year's budget deficit would exceed projections, largely because of decisions to spend more money and parliamentary obstruction of intended savings.

Access's twice-annual Budget Monitor review forecast an underlying budget deficit (that is, excluding asset sales) of A$6.51 billion for the fiscal year to June 1997, compared with the budget forecast of A$5.65 billion.

The headline balance, which counts all receipts (including asset sales) and therefore reflects the government's bond programme, would be little changed -- a surplus of A$910 million, compared with the officially forecast A$474 million.

Access said the economy would undershoot budget estimates, imposing a heavier social security burden but the government would save money from low inflation and interest rates on its debt. The main influence on spending levels, therefore, would be so-called "discretionary" measures, not the "parameter" changes in the economy that are beyond government control.
But Access said there was a risk that parliamentary attacks on deficit-slashing measures in the budget would force spending higher than currently expected.

"The estimate of the policy-driven increases in outlays in 1996/97 is conservative," it said. "Other budget savings remain at the mercy of the Senate (the upper house), and there could be additions to spending from a variety of sources."

The government has announced measures that would cut A$7.2 billion from its 1997/98 budget, but A$2 billion of those measures are currently at risk in the Senate, where almost all non-government senators are trying to vote them down.
Debate on the contentious budget measures is supposed to be finished by the end of next week but little progress has been made.
Overall, Access forecast underlying spending of A$137.17 billion in 1996/97 budget, compared with the budgeted A$135.81 billion.
Access said government revenue was largely on track with budget projections, forecasting A$130.66 billion, compared with the government expectation of A$130.16 billion.
Pay-as-you-earn (PAYE) income tax would undershoot projections, however, partly because the wages that supply the tax would not grow as quickly as the government assumed.
"We expect that various factors will keep wage growth moderate in 1996/97," Access said.

"These include modest -- and slowing -- inflation, slight rises in unemployment, the coontinuing trend towards part-time rather than full-time employment, and a period of change in industrial relations structures."
PAYE collections, the biggest single source of government revenue, are supposed to be A$57.70 billion in 1996/97. Access forecast A$57.20 billion, a $500 million shortfall.
Confusingly, however, the government's financial reports for the first quarter of the fiscal year showed buoyant PAYE collections.
Accordingly, Access said there was a risk that PAYE colletions would be stronger than it expected.
